Yes. On 16 June the plant exceeded the 1,250 kW contract limit twice, in the 08:00–08:15 window:

- Peak: 1,324.4 kW at 08:15, which is 1.06× the contract [data: get_demand]
- 08:00: 1,307.1 kW and 08:15: 1,324.4 kW — both above the 1,250 kW limit [data: get_demand]

This is the "Monday morning simultaneous start" scenario (S2), where machines start at once and the demand spikes before settling. The rest of the day stayed under contract (mean 693.6 kW).

I can't tell you the penalty amount from these tools, but I can run the staggered-start simulation to show how much of a peak/penalty a staggered start would have avoided.

According to SOP-02, a reflow oven in standby draws 36% of its 70 kW rating (25.2 kW) continuously, so leaving it in standby wastes far more energy than a properly switched-off oven (which uses only ~340–350 kWh per oven-weekend). The off-schedule rule only flags it after 120 minutes above 20% of rating, so the saving comes from switching it off proactively.

In incident S5 (2025-10-17 to 2025-10-20), RF-02 was left in standby all weekend: weekend energy was about 1,556 kWh versus about 346 kWh normal, an excess of about 1,210 kWh from that single oven.

Note: the documents give the excess in kWh, not in NT$ cost — no dollar figure is stated.

answer:
According to SOP-03 (Step 2, playbook order), the **first load shed is EV charging (EV-01, 100% of its load)** — pausing EV charging is shed action #1.

Loads that must **never** be shed: the server room, running molders mid-cycle, and reflow ovens with boards inside. [source: docs/knowledge/sop/SOP-03_demand_exceedance_response.md#SOP-03 Demand Exceedance Response > Step 2: shed in playbook order]

The full shed order is: (1) pause EV charging, (2) delay the next burn-in loading (BI-01, BI-02), (3) raise chilled-water setpoint +1°C (CH-01, CH-02), (4) lower compressed-air pressure 0.5 bar (AC-01–AC-03). [source: docs/knowledge/sop/SOP-03_demand_exceedance_response.md#SOP-03 Demand Exceedance Response > Step 2: shed in playbook order]
